A characteristic is not the danger itsel.en: A characteristic is not the danger itself: seeing Fl(2) does not prove that the light is an isolated danger mark, because another aid to navigation may use the same rhythm. Check the symbol and the position on the chart.

A group of six flashes plus a long flash.en: A group of six flashes plus a long flash is the south cardinal; pass south of the danger.

A light characteristic is the signature.en: A light characteristic is the signature that describes how a light comes on, goes off or changes color over time. It has four elements; the elevation and the range of the light complete the description.

A light you cannot see is not necessaril.en: A light you cannot see is not necessarily out of order: it may be below the geographic horizon, in another sector or behind rain or fog, or lights ashore may mask it.

A light's visibility has two limits, bri.en: A light's visibility has two limits, brightness and the horizon. Which one applies?

A sector light shows a different color o.en: A sector light shows a different color or characteristic depending on the direction from which it is seen. In a common arrangement the white sector marks the safe approach and the red and green sectors mark the limits on either side or the side of a danger. This is a habit, not a rule: you cannot assume that white is always safe or that red or green is always dangerous; read the meaning of the sectors from the chart and the List of Lights.

A sequence of quick flashes is interrupt.en: A sequence of quick flashes is interrupted at regular intervals by a long eclipse.

A single flash lasts at least 2 seconds..en: A single flash lasts at least 2 seconds.

A steady light with brighter flashes add.en: A steady light with brighter flashes added to it.

Bright blocks show the light on, dark bl.en: Bright blocks show the light on, dark blocks the eclipses. The bracket above a track marks one period. Timings inside a period are illustrative; take the real characteristic from the chart and the List of Lights.

Cardinal flash counts follow a clock fac.en: Cardinal flash counts follow a clock face: 3 east, 6 plus a long flash south, 9 west, continuous north.

Cardinal marks show on which side of a d.en: Cardinal marks show on which side of a danger it is safe to pass: pass north of a north cardinal, east of an east cardinal, south of a south cardinal and west of a west cardinal. When lit, every cardinal light is white.

Compare the bearing with the chart: conv.en: Compare the bearing with the chart: convert the compass bearing to a true bearing with the corrections, then check each candidate's position, range, sectors and characteristic.

Confirm a sector change with a bearing,.en: Confirm a sector change with a bearing, a radar range or another method of fixing.

Confirm with independent information: cr.en: Confirm with independent information: cross-check with another light, a radar range or the shape of the coast; do not accept a firm position from a single light observation.

Count the flashes: single, or a group of.en: Count the flashes: single, or a group of two or three? Is there a long flash?

Do not confuse the lateral color rule wi.en: Do not confuse the lateral color rule with a ship's sidelights: under COLREG a ship's port sidelight is red and its starboard sidelight green, whereas the meaning of IALA lateral marks depends on the conventional direction of buoyage; in Region A, entering harbor from seaward, red marks are kept to port.

Keep publications up to date: check the.en: Keep publications up to date: check the Admiralty List of Lights and Fog Signals, Notices to Mariners and navigational warnings as well as the ENC; a light's characteristic, sectors or operating status can change.

Landfall and position: sighting a partic.en: Landfall and position: sighting a particular light after a long ocean passage confirms where the ship is, and a bearing of the light is a position line.

Leading lights are two lights on the sam.en: Leading lights are two lights on the same line. The front light is lower and nearer the ship, the rear light higher and farther away. When the two lights are vertically in line, the ship is on the leading line drawn on the chart.

Light and darkness are of equal duration.en: Light and darkness are of equal duration.

Lighted marks in IALA Region A.en: Lighted marks in IALA Region A

Lighthouses and other lighted aids to na.en: Lighthouses and other lighted aids to navigation let you recognize the coast, harbor entrances, dangers and safe passages at night. The most important fact for a navigating officer is this: every light has its own characteristic, and you find out which light you are looking at by comparing that characteristic with the chart. If you see three lights at the same time, one flashing white every 5 seconds, one flashing red twice every 10 seconds and one showing a steady green, their color, rhythm and period tell them apart.

Looking towards the lights: the front li.en: Looking towards the lights: the front light is lower and nearer, the rear light higher and farther. The dashed line marks the direction of the leading line.

Luminous range from the List of Lights (.en: Luminous range from the List of Lights (NM, optional)

Major lights on the coast and the lights.en: Major lights on the coast and the lights on buoys and beacons use the same language; on the bridge they do four different jobs.

Marking dangers: a light shows where a s.en: Marking dangers: a light shows where a shoal, rock or wreck lies, or on which side it can be passed safely.

Match the number of flashes to a clock f.en: Match the number of flashes to a clock face: 3 o'clock is east (3 flashes), 6 o'clock is south (6 flashes and one long flash) and 9 o'clock is west (9 flashes); north flashes without a break. The long flash of the south mark is added so that its group of six cannot be mistaken for a group of three or nine.

On a night watch you see a light on the.en: On a night watch you see a light on the horizon. The ENC shows two candidate lights nearby: A, Fl W 5s, and B, Fl(2) W 10s. Both are white, so color alone is not enough.

On the chart and in the List of Lights,.en: On the chart and in the List of Lights, a light is written as abbreviations in a fixed order: character and group, color, period, elevation and range. The entry below is representative and does not belong to a real light.

Q or VQ does not mean that the light mus.en: Q or VQ does not mean that the light must flash without a break. It can also form a group of a set number of quick flashes, such as Q(3) or VQ(9); cardinal marks use exactly these groups.

Red and white vertical stripes; a single.en: Red and white vertical stripes; a single red sphere as topmark

Red with one broad green band.en: Red with one broad green band

Red; any rhythm other than Fl(2+1).en: Red; any rhythm other than Fl(2+1)

Rhythm is the key to recognizing a light.en: Rhythm is the key to recognizing a light on a night watch. In the diagrams below, bright blocks show when the light is on and dark blocks when it is off; use the play button to watch each light at its real speed. Durations inside a period are illustrative.

Sector limits are not optically sharp; d.en: Sector limits are not optically sharp; do not use the change of color as an exact position line.

Sector limits are true bearings of the l.en: Sector limits are true bearings of the light from seaward.

Sector limits are true bearings of the light seen from seaward. The ship on the left sees the light bearing 090°, inside the white sector 085°–095°. If it drifts south it enters the red sector, if it drifts north the green one. Illustrative values; take the real limits and their meaning from the chart and the List of Lights.

Showing a track: bringing two lights int.en: Showing a track: bringing two lights into line (leading lights) or following a sector light keeps the ship on a given track.

Shows continuously with a steady intensi.en: Shows continuously with a steady intensity.

Some national charts give the luminous o.en: Some national charts give the luminous or geographic range instead of the nominal range; check the chart's notes to see which one is given.

Standard atmospheric refraction is assum.en: Standard atmospheric refraction is assumed. The result says nothing about fog, rain, background lighting or the intensity of the light; those decide the luminous range.

The bracket is one period: three flashes.en: The bracket is one period: three flashes and the eclipses between and after them take 10 seconds together. A representative entry, not a real light.

The characteristic of a major coastal li.en: The characteristic of a major coastal light mostly tells you which light you are looking at. The lights of buoys and beacons also tell you the safe side to pass or where a danger lies. Turkish waters are in IALA Region A.

The chart shows which part of the line i.en: The chart shows which part of the line is to be used; outside that part the line does not guarantee safe water.

The definitions in this lesson are based.en: The definitions in this lesson are based on the following publications.

The elevation of a light is not the heig.en: The elevation of a light is not the height of its tower: the charted value is the height of the light source above the height datum, not the height of the structure from base to top.

The elevation of the light is 30 m, the.en: The elevation of the light is 30 m, the height of eye on the bridge is 15 m and the nominal range of the light is 12 nautical miles.

The farthest you can expect to see a lig.en: The farthest you can expect to see a light is the smaller of the geographic range and that night's luminous range.

The geographic range is about 19.45 naut.en: The geographic range is about 19.45 nautical miles. With a nominal range of 12 nautical miles, you cannot assume you will see the light from 19 miles even on a clear night; find that night's luminous range from the diagram in the List of Lights and use the smaller of the two ranges.

The geographic range is the sum of the h.en: The geographic range is the sum of the horizon distances of the light and of the eye. With standard atmospheric refraction the approximate relation is D = 2.08 × (√H + √h), where D is in nautical miles and H, the elevation of the light, and h, the height of eye, are in meters. Try your own values in the calculator.

The geometric range set by the curvature.en: The geometric range set by the curvature of the Earth, the elevation of the light and the observer's height of eye.

The light changes color; for example, Al.en: The light changes color; for example, Al Fl WR flashes white and red alternately.

The light is on for longer than it is of.en: The light is on for longer than it is off; it is eclipsed briefly at regular intervals.

The light shows a Morse letter; A is one.en: The light shows a Morse letter; A is one short and one long appearance of light.

The period is the duration of the whole.en: The period is the duration of the whole sequence, flashes and eclipses included.

The period is the most often misread ele.en: The period is the most often misread element. 10s does not mean that each flash lasts 10 seconds or that there are 10 seconds between flashes: the three flashes and the eclipses between and after them take 10 seconds together, and then the sequence repeats exactly. To time the period, measure from the first flash of one group to the first flash of the next.

The range set by the intensity of the li.en: The range set by the intensity of the light alone, in standard conditions with a meteorological visibility of 10 nautical miles. This is the range given in Admiralty publications.
The range set by the intensity of the light and the meteorological visibility at the time; it is read from the luminous range diagram in the List of Lights.

The rhythm identifies the light, the col.en: The rhythm identifies the light, the color and the type of mark tell you what it means, and the chart and the bearing put the light you see in the right place.

The smaller of the luminous range, set b.en: The smaller of the luminous range, set by brightness, and the geographic range, set by the horizon (D = 2.08 × (√H + √h)), decides.

The whole group, flashes and eclipses to.en: The whole group, flashes and eclipses together, repeats every 10 seconds

These are the common mistakes when worki.en: These are the common mistakes when working with lights.

This method lets you check by eye that y.en: This method lets you check by eye that you are on the line even without GNSS, but it does not replace checks of depth, traffic and other safety factors.

This notation follows section P of IHO I.en: This notation follows section P of IHO INT 1 (Chart 1) and the Admiralty List of Lights and Fog Signals.

Time the period by counting seconds or w.en: Time the period by counting seconds or with a stopwatch: measure from the first flash of one group to the first flash of the next, over several cycles.

Two eclipses form a group in each period.en: Two eclipses form a group in each period.

Two flashes follow each other, then come.en: Two flashes follow each other, then comes a longer eclipse.

Two flashes, then a separate single flas.en: Two flashes, then a separate single flash.

Unless stated otherwise, sector limits a.en: Unless stated otherwise, sector limits are given as true bearings of the light from seaward. If the chart gives the white sector as 085°–095°, a ship that sees the light bearing between 085° and 095° is in the white sector; the ship is west of the light.

When a light first rises above the horiz.en: When a light first rises above the horizon or dips below it, its distance from the ship is about the geographic range; together with the bearing of the light this gives a position.

When the ship moves off the line, the di.en: When the ship moves off the line, the distant rear light shifts less than the nearer front light. So, looking towards the lights, if the rear light appears to the left of the front light, the ship is to port of the line and alters course to starboard to regain it; if it appears to the right, the ship is to starboard of the line and alters course to port.

When you judge how far away a light can.en: When you judge how far away a light can be seen, keep three different kinds of range apart.

Whether the light is fixed, flashing, oc.en: Whether the light is fixed, flashing, occulting and so on
